title: Choose the visual world
question: Which direction should shape ikat’s GitHub Pages site? All options honor the light background and strong contrast.

options.label: The Exploded Service Manual
options.lineage: illustrated field-service manuals and exploded assembly sheets
options.thesis: A paper is assembled in view: source, figures, layout, and final document shown as parts with a clear job.
options.viewport: A white, open sheet: an editorial-scale heading and Try ikat action sit beside an exploded source-to-paper assembly. Markdown, editable figure inputs, and LaTeX/PDF are separated as labeled plates with leader rules, then visibly align into one output. The rest of the page reads as a service manual: setup sequence, real commands, and precise parts references.
options.risk: Could feel like a generic hardware manual unless every plate explains a real part of ikat’s document pipeline.

raised.raise: Assembly layers remain visibly distinct and authored; nothing collapses into a decorative stack.
The pipeline demonstration has one restrained stage-reveal, with reduced-motion and no-motion states fully readable.
Keyboard operation is native throughout; focus and navigation are drawn as intentional states, not afterthoughts.

options.label: The Plotter Registration Sheet
options.thesis: A plotted proof makes the central promise visible: the figure is generated as editable vector output, not pasted as a screenshot.
options.viewport: A large plotted figure sheet occupies the opening field; source and output are joined by measured registration marks. The install action is set clearly beside the figure. Below it, a compact proof path maps Markdown and data to TikZ/pgfplots and the document.
options.risk: A plotter sheet can over-focus on figures and under-explain the manuscript pipeline; the copy must make the broader product clear.

options.label: The Build-State Instrument
options.lineage: seven-segment instruments and process-control panels, translated to a light field
options.thesis: The build is a series of named states: source accepted, diagrams emitted, layout woven, document ready.
options.viewport: A fixed horizontal register spells out the source-to-document stages; one stage is active while a real code example and output fragment sit below. The Try action remains a distinct solid cobalt control.
options.case: Holds on product clarity: discrete build stages are easy to read. Loses on audience identification: an instrument register is not a familiar paper-authoring surface.
options.risk: Could turn technical state into a retro display costume if segments do not explain real pipeline stages.

options.label: The Square-Module Proof
options.lineage: Wiener Werkstätte square lattices and ruled technical plates, translated to a light field
options.thesis: Every element has a measured place: a strict square-module grid makes per-element layout and figure structure tangible.
options.viewport: A lattice is the actual layout surface, not card chrome: a manuscript region spans the grid, figure and table modules fit different slots, and the wide output is visibly assembled across columns. Installation and docs sit in the same ruled vocabulary.
options.case: Holds on audience identification: authors recognize page grids and layout constraints. Loses on product clarity: the grid alone does not dramatize source-to-output conversion.
options.risk: The strict grid could make the page feel like a specimen box instead of a useful tool.

options.label: The Try-It Setup Wizard
options.lineage: 1990s shareware installers, stripped of nagware and adapted to a clean light surface
options.thesis: Trying ikat becomes a short, linear setup sequence that ends with a working local build.
options.viewport: The first view is a single, wide setup sheet: clone the repository, build the extension, then run the demo. Each command is copyable; the final step links to the showcase and documentation.
options.case: Holds on task success: it makes install/try concrete. Loses on product clarity: a wizard explains the setup better than what makes ikat distinctive.
options.risk: Could over-prioritize setup and leave the generated-figure mechanism invisible.

options.label: Layered Papercut Roundel
options.case: Loses both axes: the roundel is not a recognizable authoring workflow and does not explain Markdown-to-LaTeX. Kept discipline: make the layers visibly authored, not simulated with shadows.
options.kept: Make the source-to-output components genuinely distinct, not simulated with drop shadows.
options.risk: Decorative pattern could overtake the product demonstration.

options.label: The Impossible Understory
options.lineage: surreal luminescent forest, translated onto a light surface
options.case: Loses both axes: its imagined ecology is remote from paper authors and the transformation remains obscure. Kept discipline: motion follows the pipeline’s order and stops under reduced-motion.
options.kept: Let the demonstration’s one stage transition follow the real build order; never animate for decoration.
options.risk: Abstract atmosphere would obscure the actual product.

options.label: The ANSI Nightboard
options.lineage: dial-up bulletin boards and ANSI character-grid interfaces
options.case: Loses both axes: the terminal grid has weak paper-author recognition and the retro surface does not clarify the build. Its canonical dark ground also conflicts with the user's explicit light-background direction. Kept discipline: all functions remain keyboard reachable.
options.kept: Make every link, tab, and command usable without a pointer, with visible focus.
options.risk: Terminal nostalgia would compete with clear product onboarding.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A conventional open-source project page, executed with care: product headline, direct install path, familiar feature list, documentation links.
canonCard.viewport: A familiar white developer-tool landing page with a clear Try ikat action and quick-start command in the opening view.
canonCard.risk: Clear and familiar, but less specific to ikat’s editable, TeX-native figures.
